issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategies node mixes avoidance behaviours with what appears to be a trigger-like cue. 'Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' is phrased as a social reminder/trigger rather than a coping strategy, so within the specified node it is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' and 'Avoid Intimacy' imply social withdrawal, which can fit PTSD, but the specific target 'seeing people that I socialised with before the event' suggests avoidance of trauma reminders tied to the past. This sits awkwardly with the selected Negative Appraisals, which focus on incapacity, moral injury, and not belonging, without any corresponding interpersonal mistrust, shame in relationships, or reminder-based social threat theme.

issues.item: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere' is possible in PTSD, but here it leans toward a broad identity/interpersonal alienation theme that is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The Threat items are predominantly hypervigilant safety-checking and pursuit fears, while the other appraisal items emphasize incapacity and violated values; this makes the belonging item feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent appraisal cluster.

vignette:
Minh was twenty-three when the bomb went off. He had been working the morning shift at a downtown bank, counting cash behind the teller counter, when the blast shook the building. He remembers the tremor through his shoes, the ceiling tiles raining down, and the high, thin scream of a woman somewhere to his left. For a long moment he stood frozen, his hand still gripping a stack of twenties, while glass crunched under his feet and smoke seeped under the vault door. Later, after the police cleared the scene and the news cameras had gone, he could not shake the image of himself standing there, doing nothing. In the weeks that followed, that moment calcified into a single, unbearable certainty: he had failed the test that mattered, and that failure told him who he really was.

That appraisal — that he could no longer be trusted to act when it counted — began to color everything. On the teller line Minh found himself bristling at small delays, snapping at customers who took too long to sign a deposit slip. He scanned faces in the lobby, his neck tight, and started glancing behind him whenever he walked to the vault. At night he woke three, four times, ears straining for sounds that did not belong. Each time he lay still, waiting for his heart to slow, he repeated the same thought: I can’t even sleep like a normal person. The irritability and the hypervigilance were not random; they flowed directly from his belief that he was now someone who could not handle a crisis, someone whose instincts had failed. And the more he watched for danger, the more he saw evidence of his own weakness — the jump at a dropped coin, the flash of anger when a customer reached into a bag — and this only deepened his conviction that he had become unreliable, that his own mind was no longer an ally.

Minh tried to manage the chaos by staying late at the branch, volunteering for extra shifts, anything to keep himself in motion. Overwork became a kind of medicine: as long as he was counting cash or balancing ledgers, he did not have to be alone with the memory of that frozen moment. But the long hours drained him. He made small arithmetic errors, once handing a withdrawal receipt to the wrong customer. Each mistake renewed the feeling that he was no longer capable of doing the very job that had once defined him. The suppression worked only briefly; when he drove home exhausted, the images crashed back harder. He had also pulled away from his wife after the event — the intimacy of marriage felt like a vulnerability he could not afford — and by the time the divorce was final, he had a new negative appraisal to carry: he had acted against his own values by abandoning someone who loved him, and that too felt like proof he could not rely on himself.

Now, at twenty-six, Minh lives alone in a small apartment with a chain lock he checks twice before bed. He still works at the same bank, though he has refused requests to train new tellers because that would mean standing near the door where people come and go. When a customer’s bag makes a sharp sound, his jaw clenches and he feels a surge of anger he struggles to contain. He has stopped going to lunch with coworkers because the crowded break room triggers the same need to look behind him. He knows something is wrong, but he has been telling himself he simply needs to work harder, be more vigilant, stop being weak. What finally brought him to a therapist was a morning last week when a teenager set off a balloon near the teller window and Minh lunged forward and screamed at her to get out. The bank manager gave him a warning; Minh sat in his car afterward and wept, certain that the person he used to be was gone for good. He is afraid of what he might do next, but he is also afraid that nothing can undo the moment in the rubble when he stood still.
